about: Exam-only questions and their stimuli for the two fixed practice exams (docs/appsych-architecture.md, "Practice exams"; spec decision 12). Ids psy-exam-<form>-<nn>, stimuli exam-<form>-s<n>, every one invented for practice. They aim at the reader-report traps: the one research method, operational definitions, random assignment versus random sampling, a statistic read in the right direction, generalizing from who the participants were, ethics the summary describes, correlation and cause, significance versus size, and descriptive statistics by hand. Every number is recomputed by ApPsychStats (scripts/lib/appsych-exams.mjs EXAM_NUMBERS).

study.introduction: Researchers asked whether caffeine taken in the late afternoon delays falling asleep that night.
study.participants: Sixty university students aged 18 to 22 (34 women and 26 men) from one university volunteered and were paid for their time. All reported drinking fewer than two caffeinated drinks a day.
study.method: Students were randomly assigned to swallow either a capsule with 200 mg of caffeine or an identical-looking placebo capsule at 4 p.m. Neither the students nor the researchers who scored the sleep recordings knew which capsule each student took. That night in a sleep lab, sleep onset latency was measured as the minutes from lights out until the EEG first showed 30 seconds of stage N1 sleep. A review board approved the study, students signed consent forms, and they were told they could stop at any time.
study.results: The caffeine group took a mean of 31 minutes to fall asleep; the placebo group took a mean of 14 minutes. The difference was statistically significant.
study.discussion: The authors suggest that caffeine delays sleep by blocking receptors for adenosine, a chemical that builds up during waking hours and promotes sleepiness.

exam-1-s2.title: Recall after two ways of studying
exam-1-s2.text: Ten students studied the same 30 words. Five were asked whether each word was pleasant (thinking about its meaning); five were asked whether each word had a letter e (looking at its letters). An hour later each student wrote down every word they could recall.

table.caption: Words recalled out of 30 (invented data for practice)

exam-2-s1.title: Shouting alone or with a group

study.introduction: Researchers tested whether people put in less effort when their work is pooled with a group's.
study.participants: Forty-eight high school juniors (25 girls and 23 boys) aged 16 to 17, from two public high schools in one suburb. Parents gave written permission and each student agreed to take part.
study.method: Each student was randomly assigned to shout as loudly as possible either alone or after being told that five classmates were shouting at the same time through headphones. In fact every student shouted alone, hearing recorded noise. Effort was measured as the mean loudness, in decibels, that the student's own microphone recorded across six trials. Afterward, the researchers explained the deception and why it was needed, and students could withdraw their recordings.
study.results: Students who shouted alone averaged 84 decibels; students who believed they were in a group averaged 78 decibels. The difference was statistically significant.
study.discussion: The authors conclude that students relaxed their effort when they believed their own effort could not be picked out from the group's.

exam-2-s2.title: Stress symptoms in an exam week
exam-2-s2.text: Seven students counted their stress-related symptoms (headaches, poor sleep, upset stomach and so on) during one exam week.

table.caption: Stress-related symptoms in one week (invented data for practice)

items.q: Which research method did this study use?
options: An experiment, since the capsules were assigned at random
A correlational study, since it related caffeine use to the time taken to fall asleep
A case study, since each student was recorded in depth for one night
Naturalistic observation, since sleep was recorded as it happened

why.correct: The researchers manipulated one variable (caffeine or placebo) and randomly assigned students to it, then measured sleep onset: that is an experiment.
options: Right: random assignment to caffeine or placebo makes it an experiment.
A correlational study measures variables as they are; here caffeine was given by the researchers.
A case study looks closely at one person or a few; this study compared two groups of students.
Naturalistic observation watches behavior in its usual setting without any manipulation.

items.q: How did the researchers operationally define sleep onset latency?
options: Minutes from lights out to the first 30 seconds of N1 on the EEG
How tired each student said they felt at bedtime on the night of the study
The time it takes a person to fall asleep at night
Whether a student swallowed the caffeine capsule or the placebo

why.correct: An operational definition says how this study measured the variable: minutes from lights out to the first 30 seconds of N1 on the EEG.
options: Right: it is the measurement the study actually used.
A rating of tiredness is a different variable, and the study did not use it.
This is a general definition of the concept, not how this study measured it.
This is the independent variable, not the measure of sleep onset.

items.q: To which group can these results most safely be generalized?
options: Young adult students who drink little caffeine
Adults of any age, since sixty students is a large sample
Heavy coffee drinkers, since they take in the most caffeine
Children, since caffeine works the same way at any age

why.correct: Generalizability rests on who the participants were: university students aged 18 to 22 who drank little caffeine.
options: Right: the sample matches this population.
Sample size does not make a sample of 18- to 22-year-olds represent older adults.
The sample excluded heavy users, who may have built up tolerance.
No children took part, and their sleep and caffeine response may differ.

items.q: What do the results show?
options: On average the caffeine group took 17 minutes longer to fall asleep, a gap unlikely to be due to chance
On average the placebo group took 17 minutes longer to fall asleep, a gap unlikely to be due to chance
Caffeine made each student take exactly 17 more minutes to fall asleep that night
The gap proves that caffeine disrupts sleep for anyone who drinks it

why.correct: The means were 31 and 14 minutes: the caffeine group took 17 minutes longer on average, and statistical significance means a gap this large is unlikely to be chance alone.
options: Right: 31 minus 14 is 17, in the caffeine group's direction.
This reverses the direction: the caffeine group had the larger mean.
A mean difference describes groups, not each student.
One study of young adults cannot prove a result for every kind of person.

items.q: What was the mean number of words recalled by the meaning group?
options: 15 words
14 words
75 words
12 words

why.correct: Add the five scores (14 + 21 + 9 + 17 + 14 = 75) and divide by 5: the mean is 15 words.
options: Right: 75 divided by 5 is 15.
14 is the median (and the mode), not the mean.
75 is the sum; divide by the number of students.
12 is the range (21 minus 9), a measure of spread.

items.q: What was the median number of words recalled by the meaning group?
options: 14 words
15 words
9 words
21 words

why.correct: In order the scores are 9, 14, 14, 17, 21; the middle one is 14.
options: Right: the middle score once the scores are in order.
15 is the mean, not the middle score.
9 is the middle of the list as printed; put the scores in order first.
21 is the highest score, not the middle one.

items.q: Which statement about the spread of the two groups' scores is accurate?
options: The meaning group's scores were more spread out (range 12 versus 4)
The letters group's scores were more spread out (range 4 versus 12)
Both groups were spread out equally, since each group had five students
The meaning group was more spread out because its mean was higher

why.correct: The meaning group ranges from 9 to 21 (12 words); the letters group from 5 to 9 (4 words).
options: Right: 12 is larger than 4.
This swaps the two ranges.
Group size says nothing about how spread out the scores are.
A higher mean shows a higher center, not more spread.

items.q: Which concept do these results best illustrate?
options: Deep processing: thinking about meaning led to better recall
Shallow processing: noticing letters led to better recall
The serial position effect: the first and last words were recalled best
Proactive interference: words studied earlier blocked later ones

why.correct: Students who judged meaning (deep processing) recalled more on average (15) than those who checked letters (7).
options: Right: the meaning group recalled more.
The letters group recalled less, not more.
The data do not show which list positions were recalled.
The design compares two kinds of processing, not earlier and later lists.

items.q: Researchers test groups of 20-, 50- and 80-year-olds once on a computer skills test and find that older groups score lower. What is the best reason to doubt that aging itself lowers computer skill?
options: The groups grew up with different technology, a cohort effect this design cannot rule out
The same people were tested repeatedly, so practice raised the younger groups' scores
The test was given once, so its scores have no reliability
People dropped out over the years, so the oldest group lost its strongest members

why.correct: This is a cross-sectional design: different age groups at one time. Differences may reflect the era each group grew up in (a cohort effect), not age.
options: Right: comparing different generations at one time confounds age with cohort.
Testing the same people repeatedly describes a longitudinal design.
A single testing session does not by itself make a test unreliable.
Dropouts over time are a problem for longitudinal designs.

items.q: A researcher picks 80 students at random from a school roster, then flips a coin to put each one in a praise or a no-praise condition. What does the coin flip accomplish?
options: It makes the two conditions alike on average before praise is given
It makes the sample represent the whole school, so the results generalize
It keeps the students from knowing which condition they are in
It makes sure the two conditions have equal numbers of boys and girls

why.correct: The coin flip is random assignment: it spreads differences among students evenly across conditions, so a later difference can be credited to praise. Picking from the roster at random is random sampling, which serves generalizability.
options: Right: random assignment balances the groups.
That is what random sampling (picking from the roster) does.
Keeping students unaware is blinding, a separate step.
Chance balances groups on average; it does not guarantee equal numbers.

items.q: In a study of conditioned fear in rats, which is an operational definition of fear?
options: Seconds a rat stays motionless (freezes) after the tone
A rat's learned expectation that a shock will follow the tone
The emotional state a rat feels when it hears the tone
Whether the tone was paired with a shock or sounded alone

why.correct: An operational definition is something the researchers can observe and count: seconds of freezing after the tone.
options: Right: freezing time can be measured.
An expectation cannot be observed directly; it is the concept, not its measure.
A feeling is the concept to be measured, not a measure.
This is the independent variable, not the measure of fear.

items.q: A survey of 300 adults finds that people who make more dispositional attributions for others' failures report less empathy ($r = -0.35$). Which conclusion is justified?
options: Blaming traits more goes with less empathy, though a third variable may explain both
Making dispositional attributions causes people to lose empathy over time
People who report less empathy make fewer dispositional attributions
The two variables are unrelated, because the correlation is negative

why.correct: A negative r means one variable tends to be higher where the other is lower; a correlational survey cannot show cause.
options: Right: negative direction, no causal claim.
A correlation cannot show that one variable causes the other.
This reverses the direction of a negative correlation.
A negative r is a relationship; zero would mean none.

items.q: In a conformity study, participants are told the study is about vision, but the other people in the room are confederates. Which step does this deception make most important?
options: Debriefing participants afterward about the true purpose
Keeping participants' names off every answer sheet they fill in
Randomly assigning participants to different group sizes
Paying participants more so that they stay to the end

why.correct: When a study uses deception, ethical guidelines require debriefing: telling participants the true purpose as soon as possible afterward.
options: Right: deception calls for debriefing.
Confidentiality matters, but it is not the step deception calls for.
Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical safeguard.
Larger payments to keep people in a study can pressure them, which ethics guards against.

items.q: Scores on a measure of achievement motivation are normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. About what percentile is a score of 60?
options: The 84th percentile
The 34th percentile
The 60th percentile
The 68th percentile

why.correct: A score of 60 is one standard deviation above the mean. Half the scores lie below the mean and 34% between the mean and +1 SD, so 50 + 34 = 84.
options: 34% is only the band between the mean and +1 SD; add the 50% below the mean.
A score is not its percentile.
68% lies within one SD on both sides, not below +1 SD.

items.q: Across 150 adults, weekly stress scores and the number of colds caught in a year correlate at $r = +0.40$. What does this tell you about these adults?
options: Those with higher stress tended to catch more colds, a moderate positive relationship
Stress caused 40% of the colds these adults caught that year
Those with higher stress tended to catch fewer colds over the year of the study
Each adult's number of colds can be predicted exactly from stress

why.correct: A positive r means the two rise together; about 0.4 is a moderate relationship. A correlation is not a percent and does not show cause.
options: Right: positive direction, moderate strength.
r is not a percent, and a correlation cannot show cause.
A positive r means the variables rise together.
A moderate r leaves much of the variation unexplained.

items.q: In a drug trial for depression, one group gets the drug and another an identical-looking sugar pill, and neither the patients nor the clinicians rating symptoms know who got which. What is this design meant to control?
options: The expectations of patients and raters
Differences between people who volunteer and those who do not
The side effects that the drug causes in some patients
Whether the results apply to people outside the trial

why.correct: A placebo controls for patients' expectations; keeping the raters unaware (double-blind) controls experimenter bias.
options: Right: placebo and double-blind procedures control expectations.
Volunteer differences are about sampling, which blinding does not address.
Side effects are recorded, not controlled, by blinding.
Generalizability depends on the sample, not on blinding.

items.q: A questionnaire asks teenagers how often they feel sad and whether they have skipped school. Which problem most threatens the accuracy of its answers?
options: Social desirability bias, because some teens may underreport what looks bad
Lack of random assignment, because teens were not placed in groups
Experimenter bias, because the researcher knows each teen's group
A small effect size, because the questions measure small effects

why.correct: Self-report surveys depend on honest answers; people may underreport behavior they think others disapprove of.
options: Right: self-reports can be bent toward what looks acceptable.
A survey does not assign people to groups, so random assignment is not its problem.
There are no groups in this survey for a researcher to know.
Effect size describes results, not the accuracy of the answers.

items.q: A study of 4,000 people finds that a gratitude exercise raised life-satisfaction scores by 0.1 point on a 7-point scale, a statistically significant difference. What is the best interpretation?
options: The difference is unlikely to be due to chance, but it is small
The difference is large, because significant means important
The difference is likely due to chance, because 0.1 point is small
The exercise raised each person's satisfaction by 0.1 point

why.correct: Statistical significance says a difference is unlikely to be chance; with 4,000 people even a tiny effect can be significant. Effect size says how big it is.
options: Right: significant and small at once.
Significant does not mean large or important.
Significance means the opposite: unlikely to be chance.
A mean difference describes the groups, not each person.

items.q: Intelligence test scores are normally distributed with a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. About what percent of test takers score below 130?
options: About 97.5%
About 95%
About 2.5%
About 47.5%

why.correct: 130 is two standard deviations above the mean. 50% lie below the mean and 47.5% between the mean and +2 SD, so about 97.5% score below 130.
options: 95% lie within two SDs on both sides, not below +2 SD.
2.5% score above 130, not below it.
47.5% is only the share between 100 and 130.

items.q: A neurologist studies one patient in depth after a stroke damaged part of the left frontal lobe. The patient understands speech but struggles to produce it. What is the main limit of this method?
options: One patient may not represent others with similar damage
It gives little detail about this one patient's symptoms
It relies on random assignment, which is unethical for strokes
It measures two variables and reports just their correlation

why.correct: A case study gives rich detail about one person, but that person may be unusual, so findings must be checked in others.
options: Right: one case may not generalize.
Detail about one person is the strength of a case study.
A case study assigns no one to anything.
That describes a correlational study.

items.q: What was the independent variable in this study?
options: Whether students believed they were shouting alone or with five classmates
The mean loudness each student's microphone recorded
The students' grade level and which school they attended
Whether the students had given their own consent to take part in the study

why.correct: The researchers manipulated what students believed (alone or in a group) and assigned it at random: that is the independent variable.
options: Right: the manipulated condition.
Loudness is the dependent variable, the measured outcome.
Grade and school describe the participants; they were not manipulated.
Consent is an ethical step, not a variable.

items.q: How did the researchers operationally define effort?
options: The mean decibel level the student's microphone recorded across six trials
How hard each student felt they had tried during the study
Putting in less effort when one's work is pooled with the work of a group
Whether the student was told five classmates were shouting

why.correct: The operational definition is the measure this study used: mean decibels across six trials.
options: Right: the study's measure of effort.
A self-rating was not collected; the study used the microphone.
This defines social loafing in general, not how effort was measured.
This is the independent variable.

items.q: Which ethical guideline does the summary describe the researchers applying?
options: Debriefing: afterward they explained the deception and why it was needed
Confidentiality: they removed students' names from the recordings
Random assignment: they assigned students to conditions by chance
Compensation: they paid each student for the hour

why.correct: The method says the researchers explained the deception afterward: debriefing. Parental permission and student agreement are also described.
options: Right: the summary describes it.
The summary does not mention removing names.
Random assignment is a design feature, not an ethical guideline.
The summary does not mention payment.

items.q: To which population do these results most clearly generalize?
options: Suburban high school students aged 16 to 17
Adults at work, since 48 students is a large sample
Young children, since effort habits form early
People in collectivist cultures, since the groups were large

why.correct: Generalizability rests on the participants' characteristics: 16- and 17-year-olds from suburban public high schools.
options: Right: the sample matches it.
Sample size does not make teenagers represent adults at work.
No young children took part.
The study says nothing about culture, and the groups were imagined.

items.q: What is the mean number of symptoms?
options: 6 symptoms
4 symptoms
3 symptoms
42 symptoms

why.correct: The seven counts add to 42 (5 + 19 + 3 + 2 + 6 + 3 + 4), and 42 divided by 7 is 6.
options: Right: 42 divided by 7 is 6.
4 is the median, the middle score.
3 is the mode, the most frequent score.
42 is the sum; divide by the 7 students.

items.q: What is the median number of symptoms?
options: 4 symptoms
6 symptoms
2 symptoms
17 symptoms

why.correct: In order the counts are 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 6, 19; the fourth, middle score is 4.
options: Right: the middle of the ordered scores.
6 is the mean.
2 is the middle of the list as printed; order the scores first.
17 is the range, a measure of spread.

items.q: Which measure best describes a typical student's symptoms in this table, and why?
options: The median, because Ben's 19 symptoms pull the mean up
The mean, because it includes Ben's 19-symptom score
The range, because it shows the usual number of symptoms
The mode, because 19 is the most frequent number of symptoms

why.correct: One extreme score (19) pulls the mean (6) above most students; the median (4) is not pulled by it.
options: Right: the median resists the outlier.
Including the outlier is why the mean is misleading here.
The range measures spread, not a typical score.
19 occurs once; the mode is 3.

items.q: What is the range of the symptom counts?
options: 17 symptoms
19 symptoms
6 symptoms
7 symptoms

why.correct: The range is the highest minus the lowest: 19 minus 2 = 17.
options: Right: 19 minus 2.
19 is the highest score; subtract the lowest.
6 is the mean.
7 is the number of students.

items.q: In a twin study of a trait, identical twins raised apart correlate at $r = +0.70$ and fraternal twins raised together at $r = +0.35$. Which conclusion do these data best support?
options: Genes contribute to the trait, since twins with more shared genes are more alike even apart
The shared home explains the trait, since the fraternal twins were raised together
The trait is set at birth, and the environment plays no part in it
Identical twins are 70% alike from genes and 30% alike from environment

why.correct: Identical twins raised apart share genes but not a home, yet they are more alike than fraternal twins who share a home: evidence of genetic influence.
options: Right: more shared genes, more alike.
The fraternal twins shared a home and were less alike.
Genetic influence does not mean the environment plays no part.
A correlation is not a percent split between genes and environment.

items.q: A researcher injects rats with a drug thought to act as a GABA agonist and finds they become calmer. Which control group would best show that the drug, not the injection, caused the change?
options: Rats injected with salt water in the same way and at the same time
Rats given a larger dose of the same drug the next day
Rats left in their home cages with no handling or injection
Rats given the same drug on a different day of the week

why.correct: A placebo injection matches everything except the drug, so a difference between the groups can be credited to the drug.
options: Right: it matches everything but the drug.
A larger dose tests dose, not whether the injection itself calms rats.
No handling leaves out the injection, so it cannot separate the two.
This still gives the drug, so nothing is compared with it.

items.q: Which hypothesis is stated so that it can be tested?
options: Students who learn a second, similar list will recall fewer words from the first than students who rest
Interference affects memory in many different ways, depending on what is learned
Forgetting happens because memories slowly fade away over time without being used
Students forget things when their minds are busy

why.correct: A testable hypothesis names the groups, the measure (words recalled) and the predicted direction.
options: Right: groups, measure and direction.
This names no measure and no direction.
Fading over time is a theory with no measure or comparison named.
"Busy minds" is not defined in a way anyone could measure.

items.q: To study how high school students solve problems, a researcher posts an online puzzle survey and analyzes whoever completes it. What is the main problem with this sample?
options: It is self-selected, so it may not represent high school students
It has no independent variable, so it is not a real survey
It is too large to analyze by hand in one study
It records answers online, so it misses students' open-ended explanations

why.correct: Volunteers who choose to finish an online puzzle may differ from other students (more interested, more confident), so the sample may not be representative.
options: Right: a self-selected sample may be biased.
Surveys do not need an independent variable.
A large sample is not a problem in itself.
Online forms can record open-ended answers.

items.q: A researcher tests the same 200 children at ages 4, 8 and 12 on conservation tasks; by age 12, 120 children remain. What is the main weakness of this design?
options: Attrition: the children who dropped out may differ from those who stayed
Cohort effects: the age groups grew up in different times
No random assignment: the children chose their own ages
No confidentiality: the researchers knew the children's names

why.correct: This is a longitudinal design. Losing 80 children (attrition) can bias the results if those who left differ from those who stayed.
options: Right: attrition is the risk of a longitudinal study.
Cohort effects trouble cross-sectional designs; here one group was followed.
Age cannot be assigned, and no one chose it.
Knowing names is normal; keeping them private is what matters.

items.q: A researcher watches children at a playground and counts aggressive acts on days after a popular cartoon airs. Which method is this, and what is its main limit?
options: Naturalistic observation; it cannot show the cartoon caused the aggression
An experiment; the cartoon airing was the independent variable
A case study; it examines one child in depth
A survey; children may answer to look good

why.correct: The researcher records behavior in its natural setting without manipulating anything: naturalistic observation, which shows what happens but not why.
options: Right: observation in a natural setting, no manipulation.
Nothing was manipulated or assigned, so it is not an experiment.
Many children were watched, not one in depth.
No one was asked questions.

items.q: Newborn birth weights in one hospital are roughly normal with a mean of 3,400 grams and a standard deviation of 500 grams. About what percent of newborns weigh between 2,900 and 3,900 grams?
options: About 68%
About 34%
About 95%
About 50%

why.correct: 2,900 and 3,900 grams are one standard deviation below and above the mean, and about 68% of a normal distribution lies within one SD.
options: Right: within one SD on both sides.
34% is only one side, from the mean to +1 SD.
95% lies within two SDs.
50% lies below the mean.

items.q: A personality test gives many students very different extraversion scores when they take it twice, two weeks apart. What does this show?
options: The test has low reliability
The test has high validity
The test is standardized
The test has high reliability

why.correct: Reliability is consistency: a test that gives the same person very different scores two weeks apart is unreliable.
options: Right: inconsistent scores mean low reliability.
A test that is not consistent cannot be measuring what it claims well.
Standardization is about norms and procedures, not consistency.
High reliability would mean similar scores both times.

items.q: In a study of facial expressions and mood, participants guessed the hypothesis from the instructions and acted the way they thought they should. What is this problem called?
options: Demand characteristics
Random sampling
Hindsight bias
Confirmation bias

why.correct: Demand characteristics are cues that let participants guess what the researcher expects and change their behavior.
options: Right: cues to the hypothesis changed behavior.
Random sampling is how participants are chosen.
Hindsight bias is feeling you knew an outcome all along.
Confirmation bias is seeking evidence that fits what you already believe.

items.q: Across 500 adults, scores for childhood stress and adult anxiety correlate at $r = +0.30$. Which is a possible third variable?
options: Family income, which could affect both childhood stress and adult anxiety
Adult anxiety, which could go back in time and cause childhood stress
The sample size of 500, which made the correlation positive
The positive sign of r, which shows that one causes the other

why.correct: A third variable is a separate factor that could produce both: low family income could raise childhood stress and later anxiety.
options: Right: it could drive both variables.
Adult anxiety is one of the two measured variables, not a third.
Sample size does not set the sign of r.
The sign shows direction, not cause.

items.q: Researchers plan to survey 15-year-olds about symptoms of depression. Which step does research ethics require because the participants are minors?
options: Consent from a parent or guardian plus the teen's own assent
Deceiving the teens about the purpose so they answer honestly
Publishing each teen's answers with the name of their school
Telling the teens they may not stop once they have begun

why.correct: For participants under 18, researchers get informed consent from a parent or guardian and the minor's own assent.
options: Right: parental consent and teen assent.
Deception is allowed only when needed and must be debriefed; it is not a requirement.
Answers must be kept confidential.
Participants keep the right to withdraw at any time.

items.q: Maya scored 80 on a memory test (mean 70, standard deviation 5) and 85 on a vocabulary test (mean 80, standard deviation 10). How far above the mean was each score, in standard deviations?
options: Memory 2 SD above; vocabulary 0.5 SD above
Memory 10 SD above; vocabulary 5 SD above
Memory 0.5 SD above; vocabulary 2 SD above
Memory 1 SD above; vocabulary 1 SD above

why.correct: z = (score minus mean) / SD: memory (80 - 70) / 5 = 2; vocabulary (85 - 80) / 10 = 0.5.
options: These are raw points above the mean; divide by the SD.
This swaps the two tests.
Each score is above its mean, but by different numbers of SDs.
